title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
hook: a widowed Moabite refuses to leave her mother-in-law: your people shall be my people

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dagon's temple, and your line was remember me, just this once.

Three widows on a road out of Moab. The book of Ruth opens "in the days when the judges ruled," and it opens small. A famine in Bethlehem. Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to Moab to find food. He dies there. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. About ten years go by, and both sons die too. When Naomi hears there's bread again, she starts for home with her daughters-in-law. On the road she turns around. Go back, each of you, to your mother's house. I have nothing left to give you.
screen: `GO BACK, EACH TO YOUR MOTHER'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: They weep. Then the two women choose differently: "Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her." Orpah does what Naomi asked. The story blames neither woman; it simply stays with the harder choice. Clave is the old past tense of cleave, to hold fast. The King James uses the same word in Genesis, where a man shall leave his father and mother "and shall cleave unto his wife." Here it's a Moabite holding on to an Israelite, a young widow to an old one with nothing to offer. Naomi tries once more, and Ruth answers with the lines this day is named for: "Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Hear how it climbs. The road. The bed. The people. God. Then she keeps going: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. Not a trip. A whole life, and a grave in a foreign country. When Naomi sees she's steadfastly minded, she stops arguing. In Bethlehem, as the town comes out to look, Naomi says, "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." And: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." Empty, with Ruth standing right beside her. Some readers hear a grief so deep it doesn't count her. Ruth stays anyway. The chapter ends at the start of barley harvest, which matters tomorrow.
screen: `ORPAH KISSED HER; RUTH CLAVE UNTO HER.`
`THE ROAD, THE BED, THE PEOPLE, GOD.`
`CALL ME MARA. I CAME HOME EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who is carrying a loss right now, a death, a divorce, a job, their health, maybe bitter, maybe not noticing who's still around. Hold them in mind without needing thanks, since nobody in this chapter thanks Ruth, and think of one way to stay close: a call, a meal, sitting with them. If you pray, pray for them by name.
Naomi. The widowed mother-in-law Ruth refused to leave, who later renamed herself Mara, bitter, after losing everything and returning to Bethlehem empty.
Your line: where you go, I go. Ruth took the harder road. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read Ruth's vow as a picture of faithful love that crosses family, nation and grief, a love that holds on when the other person has stopped hoping.

original.note: Hebrew: clave, held fast. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clave unto Naomi.

chat.says: I've heard 'whither thou goest' at weddings. Who was Ruth actually saying it to?
options: To Naomi, her widowed mother-in-law, when Naomi told her to go home.
To Boaz, the farmer she met in the fields, when he asked her to marry.
To Orpah, her sister-in-law, as the two of them set off for Moab.
chat.meaning: Ruth says it to Naomi on the road from Moab: a young widow promising an old one her road, her people, her God, and her grave.

Moab.meaning: the land where Naomi's family went during the famine

Orpah.meaning: Naomi's other daughter-in-law, who went home

Mara.meaning: the name Naomi asks for: bitter

clave.meaning: old past tense of cleave: held fast

Elimelech.meaning: Naomi's husband, who died in Moab

notes: 'About ten years' is from Ruth 1:4. The arrival at the beginning of barley harvest is Ruth 1:22.
Ruth 1:17 and 1:18 ('stedfastly minded') are paraphrased, not quoted.

Claim that Ruth 1:14 (דָּבְקָה) and Genesis 2:24 (וְדָבַק) share the verb dabaq, and that the KJV renders both 'clave/cleave': please confirm. Pointing and pronunciation of דָּבְקָה (dav-KAH) to check.
Orpah is presented without blame, matching the text; some later Jewish and Christian readings are harsher on her, deliberately left out.
'Naomi is too deep in grief to count her' is an interpretive reading, attributed to 'some readers'.
Editor 2: cut 'across the Jordan' from the hook; Ruth 1:1 says only that the family went to sojourn in the country of Moab.
Audit: "two good choices" (a narrator verdict the text does not give) now "the story blames neither woman".

Editor: the reading of Naomi's 'empty' is now explicitly attributed to some readers (it was stated as fact); 'Ruth wasn't thanked' narrowed to 'nobody in this chapter thanks Ruth'; stock opener 'the detail some readers can't get past' replaced.
